concept.name: CSRF Defense Patterns

relationships.description: Connects CSRF Defense Patterns to api security oauth2 in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) tricks an authenticated user's browser into sending unintended state-changing requests to a target origin that automatically attaches ambient session cookies.
spark.keyTakeaway: Modern CSRF defense stacks three layers: `SameSite=Lax` (or `Strict`) session cookies, `Sec-Fetch-Site` Fetch Metadata validation, and unpredictable per-session Synchronizer Tokens for legacy or cross-site flows.

concept.whyItMatters:
Whenever authentication relies on ambient credentials—HTTP cookies, HTTP Basic Auth, or client TLS certificates—any malicious website can submit a hidden `
` or `` request that the browser happily signs with the victim's cookies. A single CSRF flaw can trigger unauthorized wire transfers, email/password resets, or OAuth account takeovers. Because browsers now ship `SameSite` defaults and `Sec-Fetch-Site` headers, understanding how modern browser defenses interact with legacy endpoints and CORS is critical for zero-gap web security.
whenToUse: All browser-facing web applications using session cookies (`Set-Cookie`) for authentication on state-changing (`POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`) endpoints.
OAuth 2.0 / OIDC authorization flows, which must bind the authorization callback to the user's session via the `state` parameter (or PKCE) to prevent login CSRF.
Single-Page Applications (SPAs) and APIs that share a parent domain (`app.example.com` and `api.example.com`), where `SameSite` alone does *not* block sibling-subdomain attacks.
whenNotToUse: Pure machine-to-machine or mobile APIs that authenticate *strictly* via explicit `Authorization: Bearer <JWT>` headers read from memory—browsers never auto-attach `Authorization` headers cross-site.
Idempotent, read-only `GET`/`HEAD` endpoints (provided they never mutate state—if a `GET` endpoint mutates state, fix the HTTP verb first).
keyPoints: `SameSite=Lax` (the modern browser default) withholds cookies on cross-site `POST` forms and `fetch()` calls, while still sending them on top-level `GET` navigations; `SameSite=Strict` withholds them even on inbound links.

Fetch Metadata headers (`Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin | same-site | cross-site | none`) are browser-enforced forbidden headers that cannot be spoofed by JavaScript, letting servers reject `cross-site` state changes in 5 lines of middleware.

The **Synchronizer Token Pattern** embeds a cryptographically random, per-session (or per-request) secret in forms or custom headers (`X-CSRF-Token`) and compares it using constant-time equality (`hmac.Equal` / `crypto.timingSafeEqual`).

The **Stateless Double-Submit Cookie** pattern must bind the token to the user's session using an HMAC (`HMAC(secret, sessionId + random)`) rather than a raw random cookie; otherwise, an attacker on a compromised subdomain can overwrite the cookie.

CORS preflights (`OPTIONS`) block custom headers and `application/json` cross-origin `fetch()` calls, **but** simple requests (`application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, `multipart/form-data`, `text/plain`) bypass CORS preflight completely.

examples.title: Bypassing Naive CORS via `text/plain` Simple Request
examples.scenario: An engineering team assumed `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com` protected their `POST /api/transfer` endpoint, which parsed JSON bodies without checking `Content-Type`.
examples.outcome: An attacker's page sent `fetch('https://api.example.com/api/transfer', {method: 'POST', credentials: 'include', headers: {'Content-Type': 'text/plain'}, body: '{"to":"attacker","amount":5000}'})`. Because `text/plain` skips CORS preflight, the browser sent the session cookie and executed the transfer—fixed by enforcing `Content-Type: application/json` + `Sec-Fetch-Site` + CSRF tokens.

examples.title: Subdomain Cookie Overwrite Defeated with Signed Double-Submit
examples.scenario: A marketing blog on `blog.example.com` had an XSS flaw, and the main app on `app.example.com` used an unsigned double-submit CSRF cookie.
examples.outcome: The attacker set a `Domain=.example.com` CSRF cookie from `blog.example.com` and submitted a forged form to `app.example.com`. Switching to an HMAC-signed token bound to the `HttpOnly` session ID closed the subdomain bypass.

tradeOffs.pro: `SameSite=Strict` blocks all cross-site cookie transmission, including top-level link clicks.
tradeOffs.con: Breaks inbound links from emails, Slack, or Google Search—users appear logged out when clicking a link into your app.

tradeOffs.factor: Stateful Synchronizer Token vs. Signed Double-Submit
tradeOffs.pro: Synchronizer tokens require zero extra cookies and are trivial to invalidate on logout.
tradeOffs.con: Requires server-side session state (Redis/DB), whereas HMAC-bound double-submit works in stateless JWT-in-cookie architectures.

tradeOffs.pro: `Sec-Fetch-Site` explicitly classifies `same-origin` vs `same-site` vs `cross-site` without brittle URL parsing.
tradeOffs.con: Very old browsers or corporate proxies may strip `Sec-Fetch-*` headers, so pair it with `Origin` or a Synchronizer Token fallback.

failureModes.name: Simple-Request CORS Bypass
failureModes.description: Relying solely on CORS `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` without rejecting `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, `multipart/form-data`, or `text/plain` lets HTML `<form>` and `fetch()` skip preflight.
failureModes.mitigation: Strictly validate `Content-Type: application/json` on JSON APIs AND enforce `Sec-Fetch-Site` or a CSRF token.

failureModes.name: SameSite Sibling-Subdomain Blind Spot
failureModes.description: `SameSite=Lax` treats `evil.example.com -> api.example.com` as `same-site` (same registrable eTLD+1), attaching cookies to cross-subdomain attacks.
failureModes.mitigation: Use `__Host-` cookie prefixes (`__Host-session=...; Secure; Path=/; HttpOnly`) and check `Sec-Fetch-Site == 'same-origin'` or `Origin` exact-match.

failureModes.name: Login CSRF & OAuth State Omission
failureModes.description: Skipping CSRF protection on `POST /login` or omitting `state` in OAuth callbacks lets an attacker log the victim into the attacker's account to harvest subsequent activity.
failureModes.mitigation: Apply CSRF tokens or `Sec-Fetch-Site` to login/logout endpoints and enforce cryptographically bound `state` + PKCE on OAuth.

failureModes.name: HTTP Method Override Abuse
failureModes.description: Frameworks supporting `_method=DELETE` query parameters or `X-HTTP-Method-Override` let a cross-site `GET` or `POST` form trigger `DELETE` handlers.
failureModes.mitigation: Disable method-override middleware or run CSRF validation before method rewriting.

commonMistakes: Mutating state on `GET` requests (e.g., `GET /logout` or `GET /unsubscribe?confirm=1`), which `SameSite=Lax` explicitly allows cross-site.
Setting `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` alongside `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` (or blindly echoing the request `Origin` header).
Using `==` string comparison instead of constant-time comparison (`timingSafeEqual`) when verifying CSRF tokens.
Exposing the CSRF token in URL query parameters, which leaks it via `Referer` headers and browser history.
Believing HTTPS/TLS alone prevents CSRF—an attacker's `https://evil.com` page can still submit HTTPS forms to `https://bank.com`.

sections.content:
## The idea

Web browsers automatically attach **ambient credentials** (cookies, HTTP Basic Auth) to every request targeting an origin—regardless of *which* page initiated the request. If `victim` is logged into `bank.com` and visits `evil.com`, a hidden `<form action="https://bank.com/transfer" method="POST">` submitted by `evil.com` arrives at `bank.com` with `victim`'s valid session cookie.

**CSRF Defense** breaks this confused-deputy problem by requiring proof of **origin** or **intent** that a cross-site page cannot forge: either telling the browser not to send the cookie cross-site (`SameSite`), inspecting browser-enforced origin metadata (`Sec-Fetch-Site` / `Origin`), or requiring an unpredictable secret (`X-CSRF-Token`) that `evil.com` cannot read due to the Same-Origin Policy (SOP).

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace how a defense-in-depth `POST /api/v1/payout` request is evaluated:

1. **Browser Layer (`SameSite=Lax` + `__Host-` prefix)**:
   - Session cookie is set as `Set-Cookie: __Host-sid=...; Secure; HttpOnly; Path=/; SameSite=Lax`.
   - If `evil.com` submits a cross-site `POST` form, the browser strips `__Host-sid` before the packet leaves the client.
2. **Edge/Middleware Layer (Fetch Metadata)**:
   - Server inspects `Sec-Fetch-Site`. If the header is `cross-site` (and the endpoint is not a public webhook/OAuth callback), the server immediately returns `403 Forbidden`.
3. **Application Layer (Synchronizer Token + Content-Type)**:
   - For `same-origin` or legacy clients lacking `Sec-Fetch-Site`, the SPA reads an HMAC-bound token and sends `X-CSRF-Token: <token>` with `Content-Type: application/json`.
   - Because `X-CSRF-Token` and `application/json` trigger a CORS preflight and `evil.com` cannot read the token across origins, the server verifies `timingSafeEqual(expected, actual)` and processes the payout.

edges.description: Executes business logic only after all three independent layers succeed.

sections.content:
## SameSite nuances & subdomain risks

A common misconception is that `SameSite=Lax` eliminates CSRF completely. Three edge cases remain:
1. **Same-Site != Same-Origin**: `SameSite` uses the *registrable domain* (eTLD+1). If `static.example.com` or `staging.example.com` is compromised, it is considered `same-site` to `app.example.com`, so `SameSite=Lax` and `SameSite=Strict` cookies **are sent**.
2. **Lax+POST 2-minute window**: Chromium historically allowed cookies on top-level `POST`s for 120 seconds after cookie creation if `SameSite` was omitted (default Lax). Explicitly setting `SameSite=Lax` removes this grace window.
3. **`GET` state mutations**: `SameSite=Lax` still sends cookies on top-level `GET` navigations (`<a href=...>` or `window.location=...`). Any state change on `GET` remains vulnerable.

## Defense mechanism comparison

| Defense Pattern | Server State | Protects Subdomain? | Legacy Browser Support | Key Caveat |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`SameSite=Lax` Cookie** | None | No (`eTLD+1` scope) | Modern browsers | Fails if `GET` mutates state or sibling subdomain is untrusted |
| **`Sec-Fetch-Site` Header** | None | Yes (`same-origin`) | Chrome 76+, FF 90+, Safari 16.4+ | Must check `Sec-Fetch-Mode` & fallback for older clients |
| **Synchronizer Token** | Session store | Yes | Universal | Requires server-side session lookup |
| **Signed Double-Submit** | None (HMAC key) | Yes (with `__Host-`) | Universal | Must bind token to session ID via HMAC |
| **`Bearer` Header (No Cookies)** | None | Yes | Universal | Vulnerable if XSS steals token from `localStorage` |

## Failure modes

1. **CORS misconfiguration with `credentials: true`**: Reflecting arbitrary `Origin` headers with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` lets an attacker read CSRF tokens from `GET /csrf-token` cross-origin, defeating Synchronizer Tokens.
2. **Unsigned Double-Submit Cookie**: Comparing `cookie.csrf == header.csrf` without HMAC binding allows a sibling-subdomain XSS or MITM on plain HTTP to plant a matching cookie.
3. **CSRF token leaked in `GET` URLs**: Passing `?csrf=...` leaks the token in server access logs, `Referer` headers to third-party images, and browser history.
4. **OAuth Login CSRF**: Omitting `state` on `/oauth/callback` lets an attacker force a victim's browser to link the attacker's OAuth identity to the victim's session.

## Framework & Go/Java implementation notes

- **Go 1.25+ `net/http.CrossOriginProtection`**: Implements Fetch Metadata (`Sec-Fetch-Site`) + `Origin` checks in standard library middleware with zero token state.
- **Spring Security (Java)**: Enables `CsrfFilter` by default using `XorCsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler` (BREACH-mitigated masked Synchronizer Token) and `CookieCsrfTokenRepository` for SPAs.
- **BREACH mitigation**: When embedding a CSRF token inside compressed HTTPS HTML responses, mask the token with a per-response random one-time pad (`XOR`) so attackers cannot infer the secret via compression-ratio side channels.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Ensure `GET` and `HEAD` endpoints are strictly read-only and never mutate state.
- [ ] Set `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax` (and `__Host-` prefix where possible) on all session cookies.
- [ ] Add Fetch Metadata middleware rejecting `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` on state-changing routes.
- [ ] Enforce `Content-Type: application/json` on JSON APIs so simple `<form>` / `text/plain` requests fail fast.
- [ ] Use HMAC-bound Synchronizer or Double-Submit tokens verified with constant-time comparison.
- [ ] Validate `state` and PKCE on all OAuth/OIDC callbacks and protect `/login` against Login CSRF.

interviewProblems.title: CSRF Defense Patterns
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on CSRF Defense Patterns. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) tricks an authenticated user's browser into sending unintended state-changing requests to a target origin that automatically attaches ambient session cookies.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: CSRF Token & Content-Type applies the primary invariant and coordinates with State-Changing Handler.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, State-Changing Handler experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Strictly validate `Content-Type: application/json` on JSON APIs AND enforce `Sec-Fetch-Site` or a CSRF token.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Modern CSRF defense stacks three layers: `SameSite=Lax` (or `Strict`) session cookies, `Sec-Fetch-Site` Fetch Metadata validation, and unpredictable per-session Synchronizer Tokens for legacy or cross-site flows.
Avoid trap: Mutating state on `GET` requests (e.g., `GET /logout` or `GET /unsubscribe?confirm=1`), which `SameSite=Lax` explicitly allows cross-site.
Avoid trap: Setting `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` alongside `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` (or blindly echoing the request `Origin` header).
When to reach for it: All browser-facing web applications using session cookies (`Set-Cookie`) for authentication on state-changing (`POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`) endpoints.
When to reach for it: OAuth 2.0 / OIDC authorization flows, which must bind the authorization callback to the user's session via the `state` parameter (or PKCE) to prevent login CSRF.

putItTogether.title: Putting Csrf Defense Patterns Together
putItTogether.summary: Modern CSRF defense stacks three layers: `SameSite=Lax` (or `Strict`) session cookies, `Sec-Fetch-Site` Fetch Metadata validation, and unpredictable per-session Synchronizer Tokens for legacy or cross-site flows.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Csrf Defense Patterns before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: An attacker's page sent `fetch('https://api.example.com/api/transfer', {method: 'POST', credentials: 'include', headers: {'Content-Type': 'text/plain'}, body: '{"to":"attacker","amount":5000}'})`. Because `text/plain` skips CORS preflight, the browser sent the session cookie and executed the transfer—fixed by enforcing `Content-Type: application/json` + `Sec-Fetch-Site` + CSRF tokens.
